title: Orders due by the stock count
prompt: Planners check each stock count against the purchase orders that should have arrived by then. Write `solve(inventory, purchase_orders)` so it returns every stock line with the purchase order rows due on or before its count date.
rules: A purchase order row matches a stock line when it has the same `warehouse_id`, the same `sku`, and an `expected_date` on or before the line's `as_of_date`. A missing `expected_date` never matches.
A stock line appears once per matching row (every version counts as its own row). A stock line with no matching row appears once, with `po_id`, `version` and `expected_date` missing.
hints: The date rule only decides which purchase orders match. It must never remove a stock line.
Put all three conditions in the join itself, joined with `&`: same warehouse, same SKU, and `expected_date <= as_of_date`. Aliases keep the two sides apart.
A `filter` after a left join removes the stock lines whose purchase order columns are NULL, so every line without a due order would vanish.
starter:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F


def solve(inventory, purchase_orders):
    # Every stock line with the purchase orders due by its count date.
    return inventory
explanation: Everything goes in the join condition of a left join: `(F.col("i.warehouse_id") == F.col("p.warehouse_id")) & (F.col("i.sku") == F.col("p.sku")) & (F.col("p.expected_date") <= F.col("i.as_of_date"))`. In the join, the date only decides which purchase orders pair up, and every stock line stays. As a `filter` after the join, it also removes each stock line whose only orders are late, or that has none, because a comparison with NULL isn't true. `<=` includes an order due on the count date itself. A missing expected date makes the comparison NULL, so that row never matches. Joining on `sku` alone pairs a stock line with other warehouses' orders.
